label: Classification As A Pipeline
notes: Open by treating classification as a sequence of reductions rather than as a memorized table. The printed span, pages 438 through 458, moves from symmetric spaces to symmetric Lie algebras, then to classical families and finally to finite root data. Learners should listen for what information survives each reduction.

label: The Object Being Classified
notes: Emphasize the change of language. A globally symmetric space carries an involution at each point, but the classification becomes workable after passing to an orthogonal symmetric Lie algebra. The metric data is not discarded; it is encoded by the compact or noncompact form and by the invariant inner product.

label: Type II Is The Group Case
notes: Use the diagonal quotient model to demystify type II. When the algebra is a pair of isomorphic simple ideals exchanged by the involution, a point of the quotient can be represented by one group element. That is why compact simple groups with bi-invariant metrics sit naturally inside the symmetric-space list.

label: Type I Splits Into Three Algebraic Questions
notes: This is the main reduction slide for the compact type I case. Once type II has been separated, classification asks for compact simple algebras, involutions up to conjugacy, and centers or finite quotients. The point is that geometry has become algebra plus a small amount of global bookkeeping.

label: Real Forms And Compact Duals
notes: Connect the compact and noncompact sides. A Cartan decomposition keeps the fixed algebra compact while multiplying the tangent part by an imaginary unit in the compact dual picture. The real form is not an afterthought; it tells which symmetric space is noncompact and which roots are restricted roots.

label: Classical Groups Preserve Forms
notes: Read the classical families through the forms they preserve. Unitary, orthogonal, and symplectic conditions are matrix equations that produce Lie algebras, compact forms, and noncompact real forms. This slide gives students a concrete anchor before the root-system abstraction begins.

label: Cartan Involution Families
notes: The named families are best read as rows in a data table, not as disconnected labels. Each row identifies a compact algebra, a fixed algebra, a tangent block, a rank, and sometimes a Hermitian structure. Ask students to compare rows by how the block pattern changes.

label: AIII As A Block Split
notes: Use AIII as the working example because the involution is visible on blocks. Conjugation by the signature matrix fixes block diagonal matrices and reverses off diagonal blocks. That one picture explains both the isotropy algebra and the tangent directions of the symmetric space.

label: The Bracket Test
notes: Do not let the block picture remain informal. A decomposition is symmetric only when the bracket relations close in the correct pattern. The three relations show that the fixed part is a subalgebra, the tangent part is stable under isotropy, and two tangent directions bend back into isotropy.

label: Rank Is Not Dimension
notes: This slide prevents a common misconception. Large tangent dimension does not imply large rank. Rank counts the largest abelian flat direction inside the tangent part, while dimension counts all tangent parameters. The classification table needs both numbers because they answer different geometric questions.

label: Root Systems Begin The Finite Machine
notes: Mark the moment when the chapter changes scale. Instead of carrying the full Lie algebra, the classification starts recording a finite set of roots with reflection symmetries and integral Cartan entries. The A2 hexagon is small enough for learners to inspect every reflection by eye.

label: Weyl Chambers Choose Positivity
notes: Weyl chambers are not extra geometry placed on top of the root system. They are the regions left after the reflecting hyperplanes divide the Cartan space. Choosing one chamber selects positive roots and then a simple basis, which is the input for the Dynkin diagram.

label: Root Strings And Nonreduced Behavior
notes: Here the restricted-root warning matters. Ordinary complex root systems are reduced, but restricted roots for symmetric spaces can contain both alpha and two alpha. Root strings provide a checkable arithmetic rule, so the picture is not just a collection of arrows in the plane.

label: Dynkin Diagrams Compress Cartan Integers
notes: Explain that a Dynkin diagram is a compressed encoding of the simple-root Cartan matrix. Missing edges, single edges, double edges, and triple edges record the products of off diagonal Cartan integers. Arrow direction matters only when the root lengths differ.

label: Classification Handoff
notes: Close by naming the handoff. The span has reduced symmetric spaces to symmetric algebras, sorted type I and type II, organized the classical matrix families, and prepared root systems for Dynkin classification. Finite-order automorphisms generalize the involution idea by replacing a two-piece split with eigenspace bookkeeping.
